info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 13.3: Multi-Modal Publishing: Compiling Web, Interactive HTML, and Print-Ready PDF Packages.

name.text: 01 Question: The Multi-Modal Imperative: Why Digital Scholarly Editions Must Output to Multiple Media

questiontext.text: What is the Multi-Modal Imperative in contemporary digital scholarly editing?

generalfeedback.text: A digital scholarly edition must fulfill the multi-modal imperative by compiling into web, standalone offline, and print-ready formats from a single TEI XML master.

answer.text: A digital edition must compile into multiple optimized presentation formats (web, offline HTML, print PDF) from a single TEI XML master.

feedback.text: Correct. Diverse audiences require different reading environments, making multi-modal compilation from a single source of truth essential.

answer.text: An edition must restrict itself exclusively to a single proprietary tablet application.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The imperative mandates multi-channel dissemination across web, offline, and print media.

answer.text: Editors must write separate, disconnected XML files for every published format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All deliverables must compile automatically from a single canonical TEI XML master.

answer.text: Print editions must be completely abolished from university libraries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Print and digital are complementary modalities of the same underlying semantic model.

name.text: 02 Question: Deconstructing Medium-Specific Affordances: Screen vs. Page vs. Raw Data

questiontext.text: How should an editorial pipeline adapt textual features to the distinct affordances of screens versus printed pages?

generalfeedback.text: Effective multi-modal publishing honors the distinct affordances of screens (interactivity), pages (stability), and raw data (computability).

answer.text: By rendering variants as interactive popovers on screens while formatting them as compact, paginated footnotes in print.

feedback.text: Correct. Multi-modal compilation honors the fluidity of screens, the fixed stability of pages, and the computability of raw data.

answer.text: By forcing fixed-width 1000-page print layouts onto smartphone screens without reflow.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mobile screens require responsive layouts rather than unadapted print page grids.

answer.text: By embedding clickable JavaScript hyperlinks onto physical paper printouts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Print layouts require footnotes or expanded text rather than unclickable web URLs.

answer.text: By deleting the critical apparatus entirely from the web version.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The apparatus is adapted to interactive tooltips or drawers on the web.

name.text: 03 Question: Responsive Web Edition Architecture: Client-Side Interaction and Semantic HTML5

questiontext.text: What core components characterize a modern responsive digital critical edition web interface?

generalfeedback.text: Responsive web editions combine semantic HTML5, CSS grid layouts, and interactive components to deliver synchronized facsimiles, texts, and commentaries.

answer.text: Synchronized dual viewports (facsimile and text), dynamic reading layer toggles, interactive apparatus popovers, and commentary drawers.

feedback.text: Correct. Built on semantic HTML5 and Web Components, this layout delivers responsive, accessible scholarship across devices.

answer.text: A single static JPEG image of a 19th-century book page with no text selection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A digital edition requires structured, selectable text synchronized with deep-zoom facsimiles.

answer.text: An unformatted plain-text file displayed in a single monospaced terminal window.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Responsive editions utilize modern CSS grid layouts and interactive UI controls.

answer.text: A mandatory paywall requiring credit card payment for every line of text viewed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Open access scholarly editions prioritize accessible semantic markup.

name.text: 04 Question: Building Standalone, Serverless HTML Packages (EVT and Static Bundles)

questiontext.text: Why are standalone, serverless HTML packages critical for the long-term survival of digital editions?

generalfeedback.text: Standalone, serverless HTML packages eliminate database dependencies, allowing editions to run offline and survive indefinitely as static files.

answer.text: They run 100% offline from the local file system without server or database dependencies, eliminating vulnerability to server decay.

feedback.text: Correct. A self-contained bundle of HTML, CSS, JS, and images will open in any browser decades later without ongoing server hosting.

answer.text: They prevent readers from printing the text on physical paper.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Static packages can be printed or viewed across any device.

answer.text: They require users to install a dedicated Java database server on their machine.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Serverless packages eliminate all database requirements.

answer.text: They expire and self-destruct 30 days after compilation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Static bundles offer permanent archival longevity as static files.

generalfeedback.text: The CSS Paged Media standard enables scholars to design beautiful, paginated print layouts using familiar CSS syntax.

answer.text: It extends standard CSS with page-specific rules (`@page`, running headers, margin boxes, and footnotes) for print pagination.
